title: Box 1.03 B-Classification of histological diagnoses in preoperative core needle and vacuum-assisted biopsies
copyright: Modified from Varga Z, Sinn P, Lebeau A. [B3 lesions of the breast: histological, clinical, and epidemiological aspects : Update]. Pathologie (Heidelb). 2023 Feb;44(1):5-16. PMID: 36635403.
tablehtml:
B2 – Benign lesions

 

Focal findings

 

 

Fibroadenoma, tubular adenoma

 

 

Fibrocystic changes, adenosis, ductectasia

 

 

Mammary hamartoma

 

 

Fully recorded small milk duct papilloma/micropapilloma

 

 

Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia

 

 

Mastitis, abscess

 

 

Adipose tissue necrosis

 

 

Myofibroblastoma

 

Radiologically relevant microcalcification

 

 

Fibrous-cystic mastopathy / papillary apocrine metaplasia

 

 

Adenosis with or without columnar cell metaplasia/hyperplasia

 

 

Calcified adipose tissue necrosis

B3 – Lesions of uncertain biological potential

 

Lesions with increased risk of associated ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive carcinoma

 

 

Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or atypical epithelial proliferation of the ductal type (depending on the extent, possibly B4)

 

 

Flat epithelial atypia

 

 

Classic lobular neoplasia (LN, of type atypical lobular hyperplasia and lobular carcinoma in situ [LCIS])

 

 

Atypical apocrine adenosis

 

Potentially heterogeneous lesions at risk of incomplete sampling

 

 

Cellular fibroepithelial lesion or phyllodes tumour without suspicion of malignancy

 

 

Intraductal papilloma with or without atypia, not completely removed (if atypia is present, depending on extent, can also be B4)

 

 

Radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion (exception: if radial scar is not the cause of the radiological change, B2 is allowed)

 

 

Haemangioma

 

 

Atypical vascular lesion

 

Rare diseases

 

 

Adenomyoepithelioma

 

 

Microglandular adenosis

 

 

Mucocoele-like lesion

 

 

Nodular fasciitis

 

 

Desmoid-type fibromatosis

B4 – Suspicious of malignancy

 

 

Atypical intraductal epithelial proliferation depending on extent and degree of atypia (at least ADH, DCIS cannot be excluded)

 

 

Unable to decide whether LN or low-grade DCIS

 

 

Too few suspicious cells for definitive carcinoma diagnosis

 

 

Carcinoma suspicion, but marked fixation artefacts or crush artefacts

B5 – Malignant finding

 

B5a: Carcinoma in situ or DCIS

 

 

Classic LN/LCIS with comedo-type necrosis and pleomorphic LN/LCIS

 

 

Paget disease of the nipple without invasion

 

 

Malignant non-invasive papillary lesion (encapsulated papillary carcinoma, solid papillary carcinoma)

 

B5b: Invasive carcinoma

 

 

Microinvasive carcinoma

 

 

Invasive carcinoma (no specific type, no special type [NST], or specific types)

 

B5c: Inconclusive for invasive or in situ

 

B5d: Malignant neoplasm of other histogenesis or metastasis

 

 

Malignant phyllodes tumour

 

 

Malignant lymphoma

 

 

Sarcoma (e.g. angiosarcoma)

 

 

Breast metastasis of primary tumour located elsewhere

title: Box 1.02 Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) categories
tablehtml:
BI-RADS 0

 

 

Incomplete

 

 

Need additional imaging evaluation (additional mammographic views or ultrasound) and/or

 

 

For mammography, obtaining previous images not available at the time of reading

 

BI-RADS 1

 

 

Negative

 

 

Symmetrical and no masses, architectural distortion, or suspicious calcifications

 

BI-RADS 2

 

 

Benign

 

 

0% probability of malignancy

 

BI-RADS 3

 

 

Probably benign

 

 

< 2% probability of malignancy

 

 

Short-interval follow-up suggested

 

BI-RADS 4

 

 

Suspicious for malignancy

 

 

2–95% probability of malignancy

 

 

For mammography and ultrasound, these can be further divided:

 

 

 

BI-RADS 4A: low suspicion for malignancy (2–9%)

 

 

BI-RADS 4B: moderate suspicion for malignancy (10–49%)

 

 

BI-RADS 4C: high suspicion for malignancy (50–94%)

 

 

 

Biopsy should be considered

BI-RADS 5

 

 

Highly suggestive of malignancy

 

 

> 95% probability of malignancy

 

 

Appropriate action should be taken

 

BI-RADS 6

 

 

Known biopsy-proven malignancy

title: Table 1.03 Comparison of advantages and disadvantages of core needle biopsy (CNB), vacuum-assisted biopsy (VAB), and FNAB
tablehtml:
Needles and biopsy devices

Advantages

Disadvantages

CNB

Distinguishing in situ from invasive lesions

Biomarker assessment (for DCIS or invasive carcinoma)

Clip marker placement (target for procedure localization and for planned neoadjuvant treatment)

Cancer missed owing to sampling error (0.3% to 8.2%)

Complications (< 1%)

Underestimation of lesions with unknown biological potential (B3 lesions) depending on B3 histopathological category between 2% and 30%

Epithelial displacement

Cannot reliably classify low-grade fibroepithelial tumours (fibroadenoma vs low-grade phyllodes tumour) owing to sampling of these heterogeneous tumours

VAB

De-escalation of open surgery in B3 lesions

An alternative to open surgery for most benign lesions without atypia and when radiological–pathological concordance has been achieved

Final tumour size is difficult to assess if the VAB removes considerable diagnostic material and the lesion turns out to be malignant

Complications (< 1–5%)

Epithelial displacement

FNAB

May be used to obtain material for ancillary testing

Materials from abscesses may be sent for microbiological testing

Rapid interpretation at rapid onsite evaluation

Low complication rate (rare, < 1%)

Diagnosis of lymphoproliferative diseases and triage of material for ancillary testing

Cannot distinguish between in situ and invasive carcinoma

Cannot reliably assess atypia in intraductal proliferative lesions (e.g. to distinguish atypical ductal hyperplasia from low-grade DCIS)

Cannot reliably classify low-grade fibroepithelial tumours (fibroadenoma vs low-grade phyllodes tumour) owing to sampling of these heterogeneous tumours

In some regions of the world, cannot administer neoadjuvant chemotherapy based on FNAB results

Assessment of biomarkers on primary tumour limited by lack of reliable distinction between in situ and invasive disease

Epithelial displacement

DCIS, ductal carcinoma in situ
